A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MPA/WRA responsiveness study despite different titles and substantial reorganization. All 16 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their appendices, support reliable comparison of the text, equations, figures, and tables.

before.justification: v1 reports original demographic analyses of existing image-safety ratings and original scoring-pattern simulations, including Figures 3–7 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original analyses and simulations and adds crowd-reference results, scale-length robustness findings, and original analyses of a text-toxicity dataset in Appendix H.

M1.justification: The core MPA, WRA, harmonic-mean combination, and reference constructions are retained. However, v1 Section 4.1 explicitly clips negative MPA areas to zero; this step is absent from both v2's description and its Appendix B implementation. This changes the documented computation for negative-area cases.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix H adds evaluation on Kumar et al.'s toxicity dataset of 107,620 comments, with groups defined by religious leaning, sexuality, and age. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained prompt-image safety dataset and its gender, ethnicity, and age groups.

E2.justification: v2 adds AUROC to the guideline-reference demographic and violation-type comparisons, where v1 compares against Kendall's tau. The new crowd-reference comparison additionally evaluates Mokken H and IRT discrimination alpha (Figure 3), substantially expanding the comparator families. The four traditional simulation comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v1 resolves plurality ties toward the most unsafe score; v2 specifies random, reproducible tie-breaking. v2 adds crowd references excluding the evaluated group and micro-averaging over thresholds 1–4, plus a median-above-2 reference protocol for toxicity. The stated simulation generator also switches from rater-specific to item-specific bias. The PDFs do not establish which retained analyses were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.2 adds an analysis of reference dependence by contrasting guideline-derived and crowd-derived judgments, which v1 leaves to future work. Appendix C.3 also repeats the scoring-pattern simulations for K=6–24 and reports stable trends. These extend the investigation of reference sensitivity and robustness to scale length.

E5.justification: v1 already reports confidence-interval bounds and group-cohesion significance. v2 newly specifies 100 bootstrap trials for reported intervals and adds permutation-test significance for demographic responsiveness findings. This extends statistical reporting without establishing an increase in independent experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds crowd-reference results placing Black trisections lowest in responsiveness and toxicity results across religious leaning, sexuality, and age. Simulation values also change: downward-shift WRA is approximately 0.65 in v1 Figure 7 and 0.74 in v2 Figure 6, under revised reported settings. The 30 top-level violation rows in v1 Table 5 remain numerically unchanged in v2 Table 3.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the simplified model from F'(V_i, b_j), using shared item severity and rater bias, to F'(V_i^j, c_i), using rater-perceived severity and item bias. v2 formalizes guideline and crowd severity references and adds a statistical-consistency argument. The two threshold-aggregation proofs are retained in Appendix A; the rewritten normalization constant is algebraically equivalent.

C1.justification: The main contribution remains non-parametric responsiveness metrics. The abstract and conclusion narrow the advertised role from calibrating ratings and improving evaluation accuracy to interpreting feedback and informing alignment. The contribution list also shifts from sampling highly responsive groups toward selecting responsive raters across groups.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of reference-dependent demographic rankings, including why collective judgments may poorly represent marginalized groups. Section 6 and Appendix G add metric-pattern diagnoses, auditing recommendations, and an explicit descriptive, noncausal limitation. They recommend responsive individuals from every group. v1's separate discussion of rater distress and exposure mitigation is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly supplies a Python implementation of MPA, WRA, and their harmonic mean, including input/output specifications and handling of unused scores and absent reference classes. It also states CPU feasibility and an O(NKR) complexity estimate. This substantially expands reproducibility information beyond v1's mathematical descriptions.

R1.justification: v2 adds works on RLHF, annotator demographics, community norm elicitation, and toxicity data, including Kaufmann et al., Pei and Jurgens, Davani et al., Bergman et al., and Kumar et al. Works supporting the deleted impact statement are removed. The core ordinal-measurement and calibration literature remains, with a limited shift toward feedback interpretation and alignment.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, model explanation, metric interpretation, and closing discussion are extensively rewritten. v2 changes the title and author list, distinguishes trained raters from the dataset's experts, moves proofs into Appendix A, places recommendations before the conclusion, and reorganizes the appendices into a substantially different narrative.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column format, rearranges precision/recall panels, and vertically translates comparison curves with offsets documented in legends. It adds crowd-reference, toxicity, and diagnostic displays, merges violation-type plots, and relocates existing material. Two detailed numerical tables are removed while corresponding results remain graphed.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves v1's important untested crowd-reference limitation and demonstrates that demographic responsiveness depends on the reference, substantially improving interpretation. Appendix H extends validation to text toxicity, while implementation code and statistical procedures improve inspectability. Narrower descriptive claims better match the demonstrated capabilities. Removing exact-value tables and omitting MPA zero clipping weaken numerical transparency and consistency with the claimed [0,1] range, but the added validation and clearer interpretation provide a substantial net improvement.
